title: Linking verbs: be, appear, seem; become, get, etc.
subtitle: She seemed unable to concentrate.
summary: Use linking verbs to join a subject to its complement, and choose the right verb for descriptions (be, seem) and for changes (become, get, go, turn).

lesson.heading: Linking verbs and complements
lesson.text: When an adjective or noun phrase comes after a verb to describe the subject, or to say what or who the subject is, that adjective or noun phrase is a **complement** and the verb is a **linking verb**.

lesson.heading: Three families of linking verb
rows: Most take either an adjective or a noun phrase: It sounds nice / a nice place. But keep is only followed by a noun if an adjective follows it: It kept him awake.
become, come, end up, grow, turn out
As linking verbs, come and grow cannot be followed by a noun phrase: come to know, grow thoughtful.
Here appear means 'seems true' and look means 'seem'.

lesson.heading: appear, look, prove, seem, turn out (+ to be)
lesson.text: After these verbs we can often either include or leave out **to be**. However, **to be** is usually included before the adjectives *alive, alone, asleep* and *awake*, and before **-ing** forms of verbs.

examples.text: The room **appears (to be)** brighter than when I last saw it.
I didn't go in because she **appeared to be** asleep.
I've adjusted the aerial and the television **seems to be** working okay now.
examples.note: an -ing form follows, so to be stays

lesson.heading: Before a noun
lesson.text: Include **to be** when the noun tells us what the subject actually is. When we are giving our opinion of the person or thing in the subject, **to be** is often left out.

examples.text: He walked into what **seemed to be** a cave.
She **seems (to be)** a very efficient salesperson.
examples.note: an opinion, so to be can go

lesson.heading: get or become?

left.label: get - everyday, informal change
left.text: before difficult, ill, interested, pregnant, suspicious, unhappy and worried; in imperatives; and in phrases such as get changed, get dressed, get married / divorced
examples: I first **got** suspicious when he looked into all the cars. (more formally ... became suspicious ...)
Where did you live before you **got** married?

right.label: become - abstract or technical change
right.text: also with apparent, aware, convinced, infected, irrelevant and obvious - and always before a noun phrase
examples: Their bodies have **become** adapted to high altitudes.
Dr Morales **became** an adviser to the government. (not ~~got an adviser~~)

lesson.note: Both describe a process of change; come, go, grow and turn (into) can do this job too.

lesson.heading: go and turn: colours and things going wrong
lesson.text: We use **go** or **turn**, not usually *get* or *become*, when colours change. We also use **go** for changes we don't want: go deaf / blind / bald; go mad / crazy / wild; go bad / off / mouldy / rotten; go bust; go dead; go missing; go wrong.

examples.text: The traffic lights **turned / went** green and I pulled away.
The company **went bust** and had to close.

examples.note: but note get ill, get old, get tired

lesson.heading: come, get and grow + to-infinitive
lesson.text: After **come**, **get** and **grow** (but not after *become*) we can use a **to-infinitive**. *Come* and *grow* often describe a gradual change.

examples.text: I eventually **came / grew to appreciate** his work.
He's actually quite friendly when you **get to know** him.

lesson.text: Colours and unwanted changes take go or turn (go blind, go bust, go missing), but illness, age and tiredness take get (get ill, get old, get tired).

exercises.prompt: Give me a few minutes to ___ changed, and then I'll be ready to go.
exercises.explanation: get changed is a fixed phrase about clothes; become is not used here.

exercises.prompt: The state of the railways ___ a major political issue during the last election campaign.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun phrase we use become, not get.

exercises.prompt: I had just ___ divorced when I met Marianne.
exercises.explanation: get divorced, like get married and get dressed, is a fixed phrase with get.

exercises.statement: I didn't go in because she appeared asleep.
exercises.explanation: I didn't go in because she appeared to be asleep. Before alive, alone, asleep and awake we include to be.

exercises.prompt: In which of these sentences can to be be left out, and in which is it needed?
categories: to be can be left out

items.text: Hassan proved to be an excellent source of information about the town.
When I looked through the window, Ella appeared to be alone.
She appeared to be satisfied with the work I'd done.
I've adjusted the aerial and the television seems to be working okay now.
'We've decided to buy a Ford.' 'That seems to be a very good choice.'
What he called his 'little cottage in the country' proved to be a castle.

exercises.prompt: A few seconds later the line ___ and Marc put down the handset.
exercises.explanation: go + dead describes an unwanted change; the past simple is went.

exercises.prompt: After the spider bit Rachel her ankle ___ and started to swell up.
exercises.explanation: Changes of colour take go or turn, not get.

exercises.prompt: The doctor told me that without immediate treatment I might ___.
exercises.explanation: Unwanted changes of this kind take go: go blind / deaf / bald.

exercises.prompt: He's actually quite friendly when you ___ him.
exercises.explanation: come, get and grow can be followed by a to-infinitive; become cannot.

exercises.prompt: We soon ___ each other and have been great friends ever since.
exercises.explanation: come to + infinitive describes a gradual change, not became to like.

exercises.prompt: The holiday was excellent, despite the terrible start. Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: Surprisingly, it turned out to be an excellent holiday

exercises.statement: By 8:30 the taxi hadn't arrived and I was starting to become worried.
exercises.explanation: ... I was starting to get worried. In informal English we prefer get before worried, suspicious, unhappy and ill.
